extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, researchers and others interested in peer review integrity and publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria about running, verifying, and defending the journal peer-review process to prevent fraud (fake reviewers, citation/peer-review rings) and to improve trust and transparency in scholarly publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reviewer identities and email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the course of the investigation, the authors, co-authors and reviewers were asked to verify their accounts and email addresses provided on ScholarOne. SAGE made a note of suspicious or unresponsive email addresses and accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should verify that suggested or appointed reviewers have valid, responsive email addresses tied to real accounts; flag and scrutinize suspicious or unresponsive addresses; contact addresses directly to confirm identity before relying on reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use reviewers whose identities cannot be verified
rubrics_metrics.description: I never, ever, Ever used a reviewer whose identity I couldn’t verify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an editor cannot independently verify a reviewer’s identity (publication record, institutional affiliation, professional contact), they should not assign that person as a reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check a suggested reviewer’s publication history (e.g., Google Scholar)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use a suggested reviewer from the author provided list and you have never heard of that person, you should do a quick Google Scholar search to see what they have published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm that suggested reviewers have a publication record and expertise consistent with being a peer for the manuscript; lack of publication history is a red flag for fake reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require or prefer professional/institutional email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: I would strongly encourage (and possibly enforce) a policy in which the emails used for scientific correspondance must be professional addresses. We have received submissions from the same author, always with different corresponding email addresses; this is weird.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer institutional or professional email addresses for reviewers and authors; consider policies requiring institutional emails or additional verification for free/webmail addresses, while recognizing some legitimate reviewers use personal accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ORCID and ORCID validation as part of verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide adoption of ORCID would have helped show that the fake reviewers had no history and it might’ve helped avoid this entire situation. ORCID will later this year be supporting validation of person-organization links by ORCID member organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Query ORCID records during manuscript or review submission to assess affiliation and publication history; where possible, use validated ORCID person-organization links to strengthen identity claims (but note ORCID alone is not a full-proof validator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on author-suggested reviewers without checks
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no need to set up fake identities that could potentially be exposed; all that is required is a ring of mutually approving cronies who suggest one another as referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using author-suggested reviewers, editors must independently verify those reviewers’ credentials and avoid automatic selection based solely on author suggestions to prevent cronyism and collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize patterns suggestive of rings (multiple aliases, repeated emails/accounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author had created various aliases on SAGE Track, providing different email addresses to set up more than one account... many of the named individuals had more than one email address registered on our system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for red flags such as repeated co-author/reviewer names across many submissions, multiple accounts/emails linked to one person, unusually positive or perfunctory review text, and repeated cross-citation clusters indicating citation rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give all authors opportunity to respond before retraction/notice
rubrics_metrics.description: All authors have had an opportunity to respond to the allegations and proposed actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When misconduct is suspected, contact authors and allow time for responses as part of due process prior to issuing retractions or other formal actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction when at least one author or reviewer is implicated
rubrics_metrics.description: The following articles are retracted because after thorough investigation evidence points towards them having at least one author or being reviewed by at least one reviewer who has been implicated in the peer review ring and/or citation ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may retract articles if investigation shows that any author or reviewer involvement compromised the peer-review process for that article; maintain transparency in the rationale for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish notices explaining investigation outcomes and corrective steps
rubrics_metrics.description: SAGE announces the retraction of 60 articles... We regret that individual authors have compromised the academic record by perverting the peer review process and apologise to readers. On uncovering problems with peer review and citation SAGE immediately put steps in place to avoid similar vulnerability of the Journal to exploitation in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide public statements describing the nature of the misconduct, the scope of retractions/corrections, and steps taken to strengthen editorial workflows and submission systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must read submissions and verify the refereeing reports (don’t outsource all judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: For science, what is claimed is supposed to be more important than who claimed it. Therefore, a referee’s history is not an excuse for editors and publishers not reading the submissions and verifying them and verifying the refereeing reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors retain responsibility to evaluate manuscripts and referee reports critically; do not rely entirely on external reviewers’ reputations or automated selection without editorial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider double-blind review to reduce bias and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blind review was preferred... Double blinding helped reduce bias in clinical trials, and should be standard for journal reviewing as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting double-blind review (authors and reviewers anonymous to each other) can reduce certain biases and make it harder to game peer review, though it is not foolproof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider open and post-publication peer review as part of transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review, as I see it as being most efficient, would work best when the entire peer review process is double-blind... pre-publication peer review and post-publication peer review to be part of a new standard publishing model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine approaches — pre-publication peer review, post-publication commenting, and selective openness of reports — to increase transparency and accountability, while designing systems to limit reviewer risk and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal reviewer identities only under controlled conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the paper was to be accepted, and ideally it would have to be more than a unanimous vote, then the identities of peers could be revealed... In my proposed system, a rejection would never reveal the identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If revealing reviewer identities, consider policies that protect reviewers for rejected papers and reveal identities only after acceptance (or under explicit consent) to reduce chilling effects and retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require authorship contribution statements and verify authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: What exactly did each author do... this issue should be clarified, ie., what exactly did each author do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect clear author contribution statements at submission to help detect guest/ghost authorship and to support investigations when authorship responsibilities are questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag and investigate unusual citation patterns and possible citation rings
rubrics_metrics.description: SAGE subsequently uncovered a citation ring involving the above mentioned author and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor citation behavior and patterns (mutual citation clusters, sudden spikes) as potential indicators of manipulation; investigate when patterns coincide with reviewer/author overlaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer independent verification of reviewer affiliation (institutional linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers can query an ORCID record during manuscript or review submission to assess an individual’s affiliation. ORCID will later this year be supporting validation of person-organization links by ORCID member organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external sources (institutional webpages, ORCID validated affiliations, professional directories) to confirm reviewer affiliations rather than accepting affiliation text at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat unusual reviewer email behavior (multiple addresses, unresponsive) as a red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the named individuals had more than one email address registered on our system... SAGE made a note of suspicious or unresponsive email addresses and accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track metadata such as multiple emails per name, duplicated addresses, or no ORCID/online footprint; investigate rather than proceed when such anomalies are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume webmail/ORCID/Google Scholar guarantees authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone can create a fake ORCID account... ORCID is a good initiative, but is not designed to provide validation to real world identities. Google Scholar can be exploited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ORCID/Google Scholar as tools but not sole proofs of identity; combine multiple verification methods and exercise skepticism where data looks synthetic or too sparse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a skeptical stance toward metrics and be aware they can be gamed
rubrics_metrics.description: These 60 papers were doubtless great for the metrics of the individuals and the institution. This is a stark warning to those who wish to use metrics to evaluate research. Such metrics will be manipulated to climb up institutional league tables and gain financial reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing researchers or journals, treat citation/impact metrics with caution and account for potential manipulation; complement metrics with qualitative assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep and (when appropriate) publish peer reports for transparency and post-incident analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: How many journals, editors, or publishers have shown the 'peer' reports? Especially of retracted papers that demand a fully transparent analysis of the entire process, including the peer reports? Allow me to assist you: ZERO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve peer reports and consider publishing them (or summaries) in cases of retraction or misconduct to allow independent scrutiny and to improve community understanding of failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement submission-system security and monitoring to prevent exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigation revealed assumed and fabricated identities used to manipulate the online submission system SAGE Track powered by ScholarOne Manuscripts™. Immediate action was taken to prevent JVC from being exploited further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harden submission platforms with measures to detect mass account creation, IP anomalies, duplicate accounts, and unusual reviewer assignment patterns; log and audit reviewer suggestions and account activity.
